title: Choosing between coding agents, APIs, and other product formats

opening.headline: When the same AI model is provided in various forms such as chat, project, connector, agent, and API, I set a standard for choosing the form that suits my work.
body: There are times when a colleague asks if it is possible to attach it to an API or leaves it to a coding agent. But if it's not clear what makes these tools different from regular chat services, it's hard to know where to start. Because there are so many names, it is not easy to choose which type is right for my work.

In this class, we will sequentially look at the types of writing on the screen, the types of tasks assigned to apps, and the APIs called from code. We then apply the same request to six different forms, narrow down the candidates in the case of automated weekly reporting, and formulate a basis for choice.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: The purpose of coding agents and APIs can be explained by distinguishing them from general services.
You can distinguish between product types that meet the needs of repetitive tasks, document queries, and external app integration.
Evaluate whether the basis for product type selection is appropriate

screens.title: How are developer tools and APIs different from regular services?
screens.lead: First, let's look at some common confusions. Read the scene below and think about where to start.

visual.alt: A picture of a two-pronged arrow extending from a situation card toward the screen and toward the code.
labels: I want to solve my work with AI
Start from screen: Chat, Project, Assistant, Connector
Start with code: coding agents, APIs

paragraphs: In a meeting, a colleague says: You can just attach it to the API. Let’s leave it to the coding agent. However, no one explains how this is different from the chat service we use.

The same AI model comes in many guises: chat, project, connector, agent, and API. There are so many names that it's hard to choose which one is right for my job. If you choose the wrong one, you will end up using complicated tools for simple tasks or having to start over from scratch every time.
The goal of this class is to understand what is different between each shape and to be able to explain the rationale for the shape I chose.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Even if the same model is used, what will be different if the shape is different? We will return to this question at the end of class.

screens.outro: Now that we know where the confusion comes from, let's think about where to start: the screen or the code.

screens.title: Should I start with the screen or with the code?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Is what you want to do a one-time thing or something that happens every week?
items.answer: For one-time questions, it is often enough to ask directly in a chat window. Repetitive tasks require some form of organization to avoid having to re-include the same instructions and materials each time. Repeatability is the first criterion for selecting a product type.

items.prompt: Are the materials I need at hand or scattered across other apps?
items.answer: If I can gather it into a file, it will be resolved within the screen product. If data is scattered across emails, documents, and messengers and is constantly changing, you need a way to connect apps. The location of the material is the second criterion.

items.prompt: Will a person use the results, or will our system write them directly?
items.answer: Screen products are a natural result of human reading and writing. If an in-house program needs to receive the results and automatically continue processing, you might consider calling it from code. Interlocking range is the third criterion.

screens.outro: Now that we have three criteria in mind, let's look at the six forms one by one.

screens.title: Types of writing on screen: Chat, Project, Assistant
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare what the three forms on the screen contain and how much they are reused.

visual.alt: An illustration showing three cards, Chat, Project, and Assistant, laid out horizontally and each containing an icon.

tabs.label: chat
tabs.body: This is the lightest form of asking a question and receiving an answer in one conversation. There is no need to prepare anything, and it is suitable for requests that are completed after asking once. Instead, the same instructions and materials must be rewritten by a person in the next conversation.

tabs.label: project
tabs.body: It's a workspace that gathers related chats, files, and instructions in one place so you can repeat the same thing over and over again. OpenAI documentation benefits from project rewriting for recurring tasks such as weekly research or drafting. Claude's projects are also independent workspaces, each with its own conversation history and knowledge base. Files uploaded to a project can be viewed or deleted from the source list, and if you delete them from a shared project, they will disappear from everyone.

tabs.label: assistant
tabs.body: Like GPT, it is a form in which instructions and materials are grouped, named, and written repeatedly by the team. The extent to which you can create and share depends on your plan and workspace settings. According to OpenAI documentation, personal accounts cannot create or publish new GPTs, while Business, Enterprise, and Edu workspaces can create, edit, and publish when settings and permissions allow.

screens.outro: Now that we've compared the three forms on the screen, let's move on to the form of assigning apps and tasks.

screens.title: Forms of entrusting apps and tasks: connectors, agents, coding agents
screens.lead: The following flashcards illustrate three forms of assigning tasks. When you select a card, it flips over. Select the right arrow to go to the next card.

visual.alt: App, flow, and code icons are placed on the front of the three cards, respectively.

cards.back: This is a connection that allows you to access or operate data in external apps such as Gmail, Drive, and Slack. This is necessary when your data is scattered across different apps. It is important to split read and write permissions to open only the scope you need.

If you give them a goal, they plan out the steps and use tools to follow them through. Recurring tasks can also be left to run on a schedule. We consider multi-level requests that go beyond a single question and answer.

Developer tools for reading code repositories, modifying files, and executing commands for development tasks. Unlike regular chat, you work with code and the execution environment. Separating read and write permissions is especially important because it involves modifying files and executing commands.

The key question that differentiates the three forms is what to look for and how far to implement it. It takes different forms depending on whether you're looking at an app, a multi-step tool, or code. The wider the scope of implementation, the more important design approvals and permissions become.

screens.outro: Now let's look at the final form, the API.

screens.title: API: Called directly from a program without going through a service
screens.lead: Switch between the two states to compare who is responsible for what in the screen service and API.

visual.alt: Illustration showing the structure of an in-house program sending a request to a model and receiving a response.

states.label: screen service
states.body: The screen and functions are determined by the provider. The chat window, project, and connector connection screen have already been created, so users can start using it right away. The method of storing conversation records, setting permissions, and connecting apps also works within the scope designed by the provider. It's easy to start, but it's difficult to change the screen or flow you want.

states.label: API
states.body: An API is an approach where a program sends a request to a model and receives a response without a chat screen. The Anthropic document introduces two paths. The Messages API is for fine-grained control by calling models directly, while Managed Agents are configurable agents running on managed infrastructure and are suitable for long-running asynchronous tasks. Each model has different prices, speeds, and capabilities, so choose a model based on the model information in the document. Instead, we have to design the screens, permissions, and record keeping ourselves.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the characteristics of each form, let's read the selection table that applies the same request to the six forms.

screens.title: Selection table substituting the same request into six forms
screens.lead: Check the table below to see which form is appropriate depending on the nature of your request. There are three criteria for judgment: repeatability, location of data, and range of integration.

data.caption: Product type selection table according to needs
rows: A request that ends after being asked once
Since there is no repeatability and the material is in my hand, it is enough to just ask without preparation.
Requests that are repeated every week with the same materials and guidelines
You can collect and reuse the same files and instructions without having to re-enter them each time.
Requires data to be scattered across other apps such as mail, documents, and messengers
Since the data is located within the app, you will need a connection to access the app.
The need to follow multiple steps on one's own.
You must be able to follow a multi-step flow such as planning, reading, drafting, and executing on your own.
Needs to modify and run code
This is because you are working with a code repository and an execution environment.
The need to embed models in in-house systems
Since the program needs to call the model without a screen, it connects directly to the code.
data.notes: Even if the request is the same, the choice will vary depending on the size and deployment burden. Screen products are often sufficient for use by a small number of team members, and APIs are reviewed when they need to be run automatically on an in-house system on a regular basis.

screens.outro: Now that you know how to read the tables, let's narrow down the candidates by automatically completing weekly reports.

screens.title: Commentary: Automatic creation of weekly reports, narrowing down candidates (1)
screens.lead: The instructor narrows down the candidates by applying criteria one by one to the automatic creation of weekly reports. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: check request
steps.body: The request is that I want to automatically create a team weekly report every Friday. All six forms are candidates. Let's narrow down the candidates by sequentially applying the three criteria we learned earlier: repeatability, location of data, and scope of integration.

steps.title: Step 1 Repeatability
steps.body: This happens every week. Chats that end with a one-time question drive away candidates because they require instructions and materials to be re-introduced each week. The remaining candidates are Project, Assistant, Connector, Agent, Coding Agent, and API.

steps.title: Step 2 Materials
steps.body: I use the same materials every time: last week's report and form. A project-like format that collects files and instructions in one place is advantageous. Coding agents are also eliminated as candidates because the job does not require code modifications.

steps.title: Step 3 Location of Materials
steps.body: If your performance data is scattered across emails, documents, and messengers, you need a connector to access the app. On the other hand, if a person can collect and upload files, it can be done with just a project. Whether or not to add a connector depends on where the data is.

steps.title: Results so far
steps.body: The remaining candidates are Project, Assistant, and Connector. On the next screen, determine the final form by considering the execution level and scope of integration. Being able to explain the reason for the decrease in candidates for each criterion serves as a basis for selection.

screens.outro: Let's move on to the final selection of the remaining candidates.

screens.title: Commentary: Automatic creation of weekly reports, narrowing down candidates (2)
screens.lead: Execution levels and integration scopes are applied to the remaining candidates to organize the final selection and its rationale. Select the right arrow to see the steps.

steps.title: Four execution levels
steps.body: If it is enough to create a draft, have a person check it, and send it, there is no need for an agent to send it out himself. The smaller the scope of execution required, the simpler the permission and approval design.

steps.title: 5-level interlocking range
steps.body: If only a small number of team members use it, a screen product is sufficient. If you need to automatically run it on an in-house system on a regular basis, then consider the API. Now the need doesn't require any built-in system.

steps.title: Step 6 Selection
steps.body: Start by adding past reports, forms, and completion instructions to your project. Add read-focused connectors only when your data is scattered across your app. This way, you start with the simplest form and open only as many permissions as you need.

steps.title: Step 7: Evaluation of Choice
steps.body: Whether this choice is excessive or insufficient should be explained in light of repeatability, data, and scope of integration. Chat alone is insufficient as it repeats weekly, and an API is overkill as there are no built-in system needs. If you can provide evidence based on three criteria, your choice can be considered reasonable.

steps.title: Instructor's Conclusion
steps.body: Start with the simplest form and expand step by step as the need is identified. Choosing the tool that seems the most powerful from the start increases the management and deployment burden.

screens.outro: Now that we've followed the selection process all the way through, let's summarize the highlights.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Needs determine product form
screens.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class. The first question: Please read while thinking about what would change if the shape of the same model were different.

paragraphs: The repeatability of needs, location of materials, and extent of integration determine product form. Chat caters to one-time needs, projects and assistants cater to recurring needs, connectors cater to data scattered across apps, agents cater to multi-step execution, coding agents cater to code tasks, and APIs cater to needs built into the system.

Even if the model is the same, who designs the screen, permissions, and data connections varies depending on the form. The screen product is determined by the provider, and the API is designed by us. So it is safe to start with the simplest form and expand as the need is identified.

callout.label: standards to remember
callout.text: When choosing a format, you must be able to explain the basis for your choice in three areas: repeatability, location of data, and scope of integration.

glossary.def: A developer agent that reads code repositories, modifies files, executes commands, and performs development tasks.
An approach where the program sends requests to the model and receives responses without a chat screen.
A workspace where you can keep relevant chats, files, and instructions in one place and work repeatedly in the same context.
It is a distinction in the way the same model is used, such as chat, project, assistant, connector, agent, and API.
Anthropic's API provides detailed control by directly calling the model.

misconceptions.myth: The API is a higher version that is better than the general service.
misconceptions.fact: There is no difference between good and bad. The screen service is different in that the screen and functions are determined by the provider, while the API is different in that we design the screen, permissions, and record storage ourselves.

misconceptions.myth: The agent is the most powerful, so you can always choose it.
misconceptions.fact: Chat or Project are safer and sufficient for simple needs. This is because the wider the scope of practice, the greater the authority and approval design.

misconceptions.myth: When you insert a file into a project, the model learns its contents.
misconceptions.fact: A project is a workspace that gathers related chats, files, and instructions in one place so you can write in the same vein over and over again. It is not introduced as a function to train a new model.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The repeatability of needs, materials, and scope of integration determine the product type.
Coding agents and APIs start from the code and system side.
The screen service is designed by the provider, and the API is designed by us with the screens and permissions.
Start with the simplest form and expand as the need is identified.
